items.author: wesley@pcgamer.com (Wes Fenlon)

items.text:
If there's anything the leaders of the AI era love more than watching the billion-dollar valuations of their companies tick up, it's warning us that the software making them rich might just destroy the world.

AI is going to kill us all. Now, can we have more money for data centers, please?

Their next favorite activity? Coming up with trendy phrases that either explain how toooootally smart the next upcoming AI model will be or justify why their previous claims of imminent AI sentience haven't quite arrived on schedule.

These buzzwords and prognostications are hard to keep track of and even harder to parse. With new whoppers arriving every week, we're spinning up a running log that we can reference whenever we need to recall how often AI thought leaders contradict themselves and each other, and how constantly they move the goal posts.

We'll update this blog whenever we notice a particularly absurd, empty, or unbelievable remark from an industry whose astronomical valuation is entirely down to the dubious claim that large language models are both going to destroy and save humanity. We're starting with just the last couple months of gobsmacking quotes, because going much further back would be too miserable.

But first, it might be helpful to set the stage:

8 times AI guys declared AGI was right around the corner:

AGI, or "artificial general intelligence," is often cited as a goal for AI development and spoken of with near-mythical reverence. Here's how OpenAI describes it:

"If AGI is successfully created, this technology could help us elevate humanity by increasing abundance, turbocharging the global economy, and aiding in the discovery of new scientific knowledge that changes the limits of possibility.

"AGI has the potential to give everyone incredible new capabilities; we can imagine a world where all of us have access to help with almost any cognitive task, providing a great force multiplier for human ingenuity and creativity.

"On the other hand, AGI would also come with serious risk of misuse, drastic accidents, and societal disruption. Because the upside of AGI is so great, we do not believe it is possible or desirable for society to stop its development forever; instead, society and the developers of AGI have to figure out how to get it right."

September 2026: Jensen Huang says "GPT-6 Astra, trained on ~100K+ NVIDIA Grace Blackwell NVLink72. From ChatGPT to o1 to Astra in 4 years. AGI has arrived. Congratulations @OpenAI team"

August 2026: "Altman [said] OpenAI was 'not quite yet' there, but that by the end of the year the company would have an internal system he would call AGI"

December 2025: "Musk said that xAI could achieve artificial general intelligence, which matches or exceeds human intelligence, in the next few years, even as soon as 2026"

January 2025: Google's Demis Hassabis says "I think we're probably three to five years away"

November 2024: Altman says AGI is coming in 2025

April 2024: Elon Musk says "If you define AGI (artificial general intelligence) as smarter than the smartest human, I think it's probably next year, within two years"

March 2024: Nvidia's Jensen Huang says "If we specified AGI to be something very specific, a set of tests where a software program can do very well—or maybe 8% better than most people—I believe we will get there within 5 years"

October 2023: Google's Blaise Agüera y Arcas and Stanford's Peter Norvig declare "Artificial General Intelligence is already here"

September 25, 2026 – 3:37 PMBuzzword alert: "Pace the Frontier"

What the heck does that mean? Slowing the rate of AI advancement, because it's supposedly progressing at a dangerous rate.

When did they really start using it? July 2026

The catalyst: A statement from 1,386 employees of frontier AI companies titled Pacing the Frontier:

"We request that the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development."

September 25, 2026 – 3:37 PMBuzzword alert: Recursive self-improvement

What the heck does that mean? AI systems being advanced enough to develop new, improved iterations of the technology alongside or in place of humans.

When did they really start using it? June 2026

The catalyst: As AI companies begin to distance themselves from the previous goal post of achieving "artificial general intelligence," this has become the new promised land. Anthropic's post "When AI builds itself" kicked it into high gear:

"For most of AI’s history, humans drove every step in its development cycle. But at Anthropic, we are delegating a growing share of AI development to AI systems themselves, which is speeding up our work.

"Taken far enough, and given enough compute, that trend points to an AI system capable of fully autonomously designing and developing its own successor. This is called recursive self-improvement. We are not there yet, and recursive self-improvement is not inevitable. But it could come sooner than most institutions are prepared for."

items.title: Nippon Ichi, NIS America Head Says Company Is ‘Researching’ AI But Personally Doesn’t Think It Will Make Development Faster
items.author: Rebekah Valentine

items.text:
As more and more game companies are growing a little bolder about just straight-up admitting that huge chunks of their games are AI generated, there are still some exhibiting a bit more caution. One of those appears to be Nippon Ichi Software, developer of Disgaea and publisher of series like Trails and Ys.

I spoke to Nippon Ichi CEO and NIS America president Kenzo Saruhashi at PAX West a few weeks ago, during which time I asked him about AI, first just as a follow-up to a question about translation and localization of the company’s games. Saruhashi was recently appointed president of NIS America in addition to his role as CEO of Nippon Ichi, and one of the aims of that is for the two branches of the company to become more unified and ultimately release more games in the West. Saruhashi told me this includes trying to release more games simultaneously worldwide, instead of delaying Western releases until months after they’re out in Japan. But doing that requires ramping up localization capabilities within the company.

Given the current climate, it might be tempting to jump to using generative AI for this sort of thing. Other companies are certainly talking big games about it lately, though at least in anime its use has been both wildly unpopular and also frequently very, very wrong. So I asked Saruhashi if the company was currently using AI for localization, and here’s what he said:

We are not specifically at the moment. But we are researching it, because we know that there are a lot of companies right now that are utilizing AI, and it’s not necessarily that we would just allow AI to completely take over the responsibility for localization or anything of that nature, but more in order to ensure the quality. We want to make sure that we can ensure the quality is there at the same time if we were to use it. So right now we’re in a researching phase to see whether that’s something that’s possible. Personally, I don’t think that it’s necessarily just that utilizing AI will necessarily make things faster.

I followed up: Does this philosophy apply to all aspects of his business? It seems it largely does:

Well, let me start by saying that I can definitely feel there’s a certain sense of pressure in the creative industry as a whole that we’re all feeling from AI. What I’m hearing a lot as I discussed this matter with other developers and hearing what they’re saying is really that for us, the end goal is really just to make a quality game for the fans. And in the midst of that, we can’t simply ignore AI entirely. And so we do at least have to research it as a possibility moving forward, and I agree with that sentiment. I think if you were to apply AI, the best way to do so would be in a way that actually improves the quality of the game, so we’re not just looking at it specifically from an efficiency standpoint. I don’t think that’s really the way to look at it. You should look at it as, “does it improve the quality of the end product?”

Admittedly, “researching” has, for many companies, been the very first step into full-on AI content creation, especially at Japanese game studios, so regard all this with some skepticism (still reeling from the Level-5 AI use over here!). But at least for now I can take a deep breath and give Village in the Shade a shot without worry.

items.author: Andy Edser

items.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has appeared on The Ezra Klein Show to discuss AI development, amid a wider discussion around its responsible usage and safety. Klein spoke to the Nvidia chief about multiple topics, including the AI industry's potential effects on the job market. "I tend to be a bit of a skeptic on mass job loss, but I want to air the case for it out here with you well," says Klein.

Klein then asks a question about lessons that could be learned from the past, regarding protecting US jobs from Mexico and China, and the acceleration of AI's ability to be slotted into new roles: "So the lessons of the past that you’re taking some comfort in, they should actually make you more, not less, worried about the future."

"I’m always worried about the future," Huang responds. "That’s why I work so hard. I’m a, if you will, responsible optimist.

"I have great responsibilities. I take my work extremely seriously. There are a lot of things that can go wrong. We’re pushing across every layer of the technology stack. Everything is hard," Huang continues.

"But it turns out that’s not society’s problem, that’s my problem. For society, what they should know is this: We’re going to build our company, we’re going to build our technology, I’m going to do my work so incredibly seriously that what they get to enjoy is my optimism. I do the same with my children. I do the same with my family."

(Image credit: Nvidia)Certainly, the current AI debate seems to be dominated by an unease surrounding the potential negative impacts of the rapid advancement of the tech, from job losses to cybersecurity concerns. However, Huang seems to think that the upsides of this speedy development process might put some people's minds at ease.

"What we want to do, I believe," said Huang, "is to channel all of our worries into helping people be inspired by this technology and use it. Use it so that the technology doesn’t just impact them, that it benefits them."

After Klein posited the statistic that 79% of American think AI will reduce the number of jobs, and that AI advancement means the tech is more capable of replacing people at speed, Huang responds:

"That coin has exactly two sides. Because the technology is so capable and because it’s so smart, it is also easier to use. You are empowered by that technology more easily than any technology in human history."

The Nvidia CEO then goes on to give an example of how computers use specialised coding languages, but now, thanks to AI, "You just have to speak human."

(Image credit: JOSH EDELSON / AFP via Getty Images)"So my point is, on the one hand, yes, there’s the fear of this incredible technology change and how quickly it’s happening. But that quickly is translated in two ways," says Huang.

"When I hear that the technology’s happening quickly, and therefore it should give me anxiety — that’s one way to receive it. The other way to receive it is that it’s advancing so quickly, it’s easier to use. So I should, as quickly as possible, use the technology so that I benefit from this transition, so you benefit from this new industry, and not just be impacted by it."

The inference here feels similar to an idea Huang has expressed previously: those who fail to get on the AI train may end up being left behind. I think the key point, however, is the lack of agency and control individuals feel towards this technological revolution, something that is unlikely to be assuaged by more useful tech—or Huang's optimism, for that matter.

While the Nvidia CEO famously possesses a massive work ethic, and responsible AI usage is a concern he seems to take seriously, I'm not particularly comfortable with the idea that our future seems destined to be shaped by AI tech leaders, and that we should rest easy within their hands.

While Huang may well believe that he has society's best interests in mind, the messaging here hasn't exactly put my own concerns to rest. Stop worrying and learn to love the machine? Something like that, anyway.

Writing from the Chicagoland area in Illinois, Robert is an avid movie watcher and will take just about any excuse to find time to go to his local movie theaters. Robert graduated from Bradley University with degrees in Journalism and Game Design with a minor in Film Studies. Robert tries his best to keep up with all the latest movie releases, from those released in theaters to those released on streaming. While he doesn't always keep up with the latest TV shows, he makes it a goal to watch nearly every major new release possible. He has been honing his craft and following any and all movie news all his life, leading up to now, where he has a vast knowledge of film and film history. He also logs every movie that he watches on his Letterboxd page, and has hosted a weekly online movie night with his closest friends for over 6 years.

Video games as an art form reached new heights of popularity and success in the 2010s, cementing them as the dominant artistic medium and entertainment industry of the 21st century and beyond. However, for all of the great successes and monumental growth that gaming saw during the era, it wasn't without its failures and pitfalls, as there were also several games that were infamously disastrous in their lack of quality. These bad games took all styles of forms, ranging from poorly executed ideas to games crippled by rushed development and crunch.

It reaches a point where many of these games have earned a reputation not for any potential qualities, but as some of the worst gaming experiences of the era. Ranging from those entirely forgotten due to their mediocrity to games that are unforgettably infamous as some of the worst games of all time, these unfortunate icons of gaming failure are the absolute worst that the 2010s have to offer.

10
'Amy' (2012)

One specific archetype of gaming release that saw massive prominence and growth in the 2010s was the lower-budget, digital-exclusive downloadable title. While games like The Walking Dead and Bastion found great success through this format, Amy was an often-forgotten relic of failure attempting to capitalize on survival horror trends of the era. The game's primary selling point is its dual player characters, utilizing the duo of Lana and young girl Amy to solve puzzles and quietly navigate around deadly monsters.

Considering the fact that the entire game centers around the importance of keeping this child safe and the relationship of the two leads, it makes it all the more egregious that the gameplay elements involving Amy are notoriously annoying and arduous to complete. Throughout the course of the game, it manages to accomplish the complete opposite goal by making the player detest and be enraged by Amy's poorly made AI. It also certainly doesn't help that the scares aren't effective, the story is incredibly generic, and it just doesn't run well on either the PS3 or Xbox 360.

9
'Paper Mario: Sticker Star' (2012)

While not as immediately recognizable as other Mario games, the Paper Mario series has carved out a niche for itself thanks to the charm of its paper craft aesthetic and the simple fun of its gameplay. However, Paper Mario: Sticker Star completely forgoes the previous strengths of the series to create one of the largest dips in quality for any Nintendo franchise. While previous Paper Mario games created their own vast worlds with original characters and stories, Sticker Star abandons this for the basic Super Mario aesthetic that, while fun in a platforming setting, wasn't interesting to see in Paper Mario.

Even worse than these aesthetic choices is the game's primary combat mechanic, as instead of a simple yet layered RPG system or a fun 2D platformer in Super Paper Mario, Sticker Star's entire combat relies upon the collectible stickers. It's a JRPG without any XP, making every non-required fight an absolute waste of both time and resources. Its fights act more as puzzles instead of actual fights, yet when the puzzles are either incredibly easy or impossibly archaic to understand, the entire game becomes a test of patience and frustration.

8
'Umbrella Corps' (2016)

The continuous balancing act that has been done between the horror and action elements of the Resident Evil franchise has resulted in several misaligned failures that completely misunderstood the appeal and strengths of this franchise. However, none of these misfires are more infamous than Umbrella Corps, a tactical shooter that combines competitive multiplayer with zombies for an absolutely horrendous final product. The game had hopes of following in the footsteps of games like Rainbow Six Siege, yet no singular Resident Evil fan wanted a generic multiplayer shooter out of the franchise.

It's an incredibly forgettable first-person shooter game that has inklings of Resident Evil sprinkles placed over it, creating an experience that was never going to appeal to either Resident Evil fans or fans of traditional tactical shooters. With no interest in the game resulting in a hilariously low player count, the game failed as soon as it launched. Ironically, the game released a week after the announcement of Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, immediately painting the game as this awkward final reminder of when Resident Evil cared more about action than horror.

7
'Aliens: Colonial Marines' (2013)

Licensed tie-in video games are always a mixed bag of quality, yet Aliens: Colonial Marines in the lead-up to its release showed so much promise that gamers were expecting it to be one of the very best tie-in games. However, the game instead became one of the greatest examples of false advertising in video game history, with the final game having considerably worse graphics quality than trailers and even demos sent to the press.

Combined with an overwhelming amount of technical problems and bugs that made the game near-unplayable and an incredibly short length, Colonial Marines was the type of disastrous disappointment that sent ripples throughout the entire industry. It had some of the largest controversies and anger from fans of any video game of the 2010s, with there even being an attempted lawsuit being filed due to its false advertising. Hilariously enough, several of the game's flaws stemmed from developers Gearbox Software prioritizing the next game on this list instead of Colonial Marines.

6
'Duke Nukem Forever' (2011)

For over 14 years, Duke Nukem Forever has stood as this absolute icon of video game delays and the immediate go-to example of development hell and a game that was seemingly never going to be released. As it changed engines, developers, and platforms over the years, the game managed to finally get finished in 2011, when it not only disappointed fans but felt outright embarrassing to witness. It became immediately apparent that the crass humor and simplistic FPS gameplay that worked wonders in the 90s simply didn't land nearly as well in the 2010s.

The game did surprisingly little to update the series and evolve it into the age of modern gaming, simply hoping that nostalgia and generic parody would be enough to entice long-time fans of this classic video game icon. Generic gameplay, tired clichés, and dated unfunny humor only served to annoy many modern gamers instead of charming them. It ended up being the final nail in the coffin for Duke as a character, as there hasn't been another Duke Nukem release in the 15 years since this game's monumental failure.

Which Iconic Universe Do You Belong in the Most?
Star Wars · Lord of the Rings · Harry Potter · Game of Thrones · Star Trek

Five legendary universes. Five completely different visions of what the world could be — or already was. One of them is the world your instincts, your values, and your particular way of existing were built for. Eight questions will tell you which one.

🚀Star Wars

💍Lord of the Rings

🧙Harry Potter

👑Game of Thrones

🖖Star Trek

FIND YOUR UNIVERSE →

01

What gives your life its deepest sense of meaning?
Every universe is built around a different answer to this question.

ABeing part of something larger than myself — a cause, a rebellion, a fight for freedom that outlasts me.
BThe journey itself — the places I'll go, the companions beside me, the world I'll discover on the way.
CLearning — unlocking what I'm capable of, understanding the world's hidden mechanics, growing into something more.
DLegacy — the name I leave behind, the power I build, the mark I make before the world moves on without me.
EUnderstanding — exploring what exists beyond the horizon and asking what it means to be alive in a universe this vast.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

Which kind of world do you most want to inhabit?
The environment shapes who you become. Choose carefully.

AA galaxy of planets, each with its own culture — connected by conflict, trade, and the Force.
BAncient lands of breathtaking beauty, deep history, and a creeping darkness at the edges.
CA world hidden inside our own — full of wonder, community, and magic waiting to be learned.
DA brutal, beautiful continent where power is everything and every alliance is a calculation.
EA future where humanity has reached the stars — and must decide what kind of species it wants to be.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

How do you prefer your conflicts resolved?
The shape of a world's conflicts tells you everything about its soul.

AThrough sacrifice and courage — someone has to make the impossible choice so others don't have to.
BThrough fellowship — the impossible becomes possible when the right people walk the same road.
CThrough growth — confronting what you fear, understanding what you lack, and becoming equal to the challenge.
DThrough strategy — outthinking, outmaneuvering, positioning yourself so the outcome was never in doubt.
EThrough dialogue — finding the third option, the peaceful resolution, the answer that doesn't require a body count.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

Who do you want beside you when things get difficult?
Your ideal companions reveal the world you were made for.

AA small crew — a pilot, a rogue, a warrior — each broken in their own way, unbeatable together.
BA fellowship of different kinds of people, bound by purpose and deepened by the long road.
CFriends who grew up alongside me — who knew me before I knew myself, and stayed anyway.
DAllies whose loyalty I've earned — and tested — and whose ambitions align with mine, for now.
EA crew of brilliant, curious, principled people from every corner of known space.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

What is your relationship with power?
How you seek, wield, or resist power is the map of who you are.

AI want to use it to protect — and I'm terrified of what I might become if I'm not careful.
BI distrust it. The most important power in this story is the courage to give it up.
CI want to earn it — through knowledge, through effort, through becoming someone worthy of it.
DI want to wield it. Preferably before someone else decides to wield it against me.
EI want to understand it — its structures, its limits, its ethical dimensions. Power without accountability is the real threat.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

How does your universe treat good and evil?
A world's moral architecture tells you more about it than any map.

AThere is a dark side and a light side — and the choice between them is always present, always personal.
BEvil is real and ancient and patient — and goodness, however small, is the only thing that can undo it.
CGood and evil are real, but they live inside people — and people are complicated, always capable of both.
DGood and evil are mostly a matter of perspective and proximity. Power is the only honest currency.
EEvil is usually the result of ignorance, fear, or broken systems — and understanding it is the first step to solving it.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

What role would you naturally fall into?
Every universe has archetypes. Which one fits you without trying?

AThe reluctant hero — ordinary origins, extraordinary moment, changed forever by the choice to act.
BThe unlikely carrier — the one nobody expected to matter most, quietly bearing the weight of everything.
CThe student — not yet who I'll become, learning through every mistake, growing into something the world needs.
DThe player — sharp enough to see the game for what it is, ambitious enough to try to win it.
EThe explorer — drawn to the unknown, driven by curiosity, most alive when standing somewhere no one has stood before.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

What do you ultimately believe about the future?
The answer to this is the clearest window into which universe already lives inside you.

AThat hope is real — that even in the darkest galaxy, a new hope is always possible.
CThat even the smallest person can change the course of the future, if they have the courage to try.
CThat love and friendship and doing what's right will matter in the end, even when everything says otherwise.
DThat the wheel keeps turning — that power shifts, winters end, and what endures is those willing to fight for it.
EThat humanity — or whatever we become — is capable of extraordinary things, if we choose to be.

REVEAL MY UNIVERSE →

Your Universe Has Been Chosen
You Belong In…

Your answers point to the iconic universe your values, your instincts, and your particular way of seeing the world were built for. This is where you would find your people — and your purpose.

A Galaxy Far, Far Away

Star Wars

You believe in the cause — in the idea that freedom is worth fighting for even when the odds are impossible and the empire is vast.

You are drawn to the moral clarity of a universe where hope itself is a form of resistance.

You'd find your people in the Rebellion — a ragtag coalition of true believers held together by conviction more than resources.

Star Wars is fundamentally a story about ordinary people choosing to matter in an extraordinary conflict — and that is exactly your kind of story.

The Force may or may not be with you. But the will to use it for something larger than yourself certainly is.

Middle-earth

Lord of the Rings

You understand, in the deepest part of yourself, that the journey matters as much as the destination — and that the world's beauty is worth protecting even at great cost.

Middle-earth is a world of ancient wonder, deep friendship, and a darkness that only retreats when enough small acts of courage accumulate.

You would thrive here because you value the fellowship more than the glory — the road more than the arrival.

Tolkien's universe rewards patience, loyalty, and the willingness to carry something heavy across a very long distance.

Those are not burdens to you. They are simply how you move through the world.

The Wizarding World

Harry Potter

You believe that love, loyalty, and doing what's right are not naive sentiments — they are the most powerful forces in any world, magical or otherwise.

The Wizarding World is a place of wonder hidden in plain sight, where learning is transformative and the bonds you form at school follow you into every battle.

You would flourish here because you take both the magic and the friendships seriously — and you understand that one without the other is incomplete.

Harry Potter's universe ultimately rewards those who choose to stand for something even when standing is terrifying.

That choice — made quietly, without guarantee — is something you understand completely.

Westeros · The Known World

Game of Thrones

You see the world clearly — its power structures, its hypocrisies, its brutal arithmetic — and you are not paralysed by that clarity. You use it.

Westeros is a world that rewards intelligence, adaptability, and the willingness to understand that every alliance is also a negotiation.

You would survive here — possibly thrive here — because you don't confuse the world as it is with the world as you'd like it to be.

Game of Thrones is a story about what happens when the idealists and the realists collide. You are sharp enough to know which one lasts longer.

Winter always comes. You are already prepared.

The United Federation of Planets

Star Trek

You believe the future is worth building — that curiosity, cooperation, and the expansion of understanding are not just ideals but the most practical path forward for any civilisation.

Star Trek is a universe where the questions matter as much as the answers, and where encountering something utterly alien is cause for wonder rather than fear.

You would belong here because you are fundamentally optimistic about what intelligence and decency can achieve — while being honest about how hard that achievement is.

The Federation is the universe's most ambitious thought experiment: what if we actually got better?

You don't just hope that's possible. You think it's the only thing worth working toward.

↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

5
'Wreck-It Ralph' (2012)

Considering the fact that the fan-favorite Disney movie's entire concept and inception revolves around the fun and creativity of video games, it's all the more iconic and painful that the video game adaptation of Wreck-It Ralph is so abysmal in its execution. It's the clearest example of a cheap, made-for-profit movie tie-in game that the 2010s have to offer, with laughably bad cutscenes and the entire game able to be beaten in a few hours.

It certainly wants to pay tribute to some of the same 2D platformers that inspired the original movie, yet without any understanding of what made these games so great, the final product is a painfully generic mess of ideas that is forgotten by the time the credits roll. There is a sardonic humor to be had in the video game adaptation in a movie about video games being so poorly made, but even worse is the fact that this game wasn't even memorable in its lack of quality.

4
'Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 5' (2015)

The Tony Hawk's Pro Skater franchise was a pillar of quality in the early 2000s, at the apex of skateboarding video games and perfectly paralleling the renegade skater culture of the era. However, much like the declining popularity of skateboarding culture, the franchise largely fell out of popularity in the 2010s, with Activision releasing Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 5 at the literal last minute before their licensing deal with Tony Hawk would expire.

As a result, Pro Skater 5 was hastily put together in a few months and released in a completely unfinished state, completely bastardizing a fan-favorite franchise and spitting in the face of fans who were waiting years for a new game in the series. It's an embarrassing case of profit-maximizing not only getting in the way of a game's success, but acting as the only reason for the game's very existence, creating a soulless husk of gaming and an incredibly disappointing sequel.

3
'Sonic Free Riders' (2010)

One seemingly inescapable trend of 2010s gaming that has largely gone by the wayside is the abundance of motion controls. Through the Nintendo Wii, PlayStation Move, and Xbox Kinect, every gaming studio was trying to create experiences tailored to non-gamers with physical motion as the main method of gameplay. While there were certainly games that found success, many failed to adapt to the concept, with one of the worst examples of such being Sonic Free Riders, a racing game requiring Kinect motion controls to play.

An unlikely candidate for what could be the worst game in the Sonic the Hedgehog franchise, Sonic Free Riders isn't just poorly made in its implementation of Kinect controls, but is outright unplayable with how unresponsive this control scheme is. Especially for a racing series that was previously defined by precision and slick tricks, the motion controls slow the feel of the game down to a crawl and make it an arduous task to even move.

While Metal Gear is massively celebrated as one of the greatest video game franchises out there, a great deal of its success and ingenuity is attributed to series creator Hideo Kojima. This meant that the separation of Kojima and Konami in 2015 placed the series in a state of unknown limbo, as it wouldn't be known what would happen to the series without Kojima's leadership. The answer ended up being Metal Gear Survive, which was worse than even the lowest expectations of what Metal Gear without Kojima would be.

Metal Gear Survive is a survival action game with tower-defense elements and minor stealth elements where the player explores a world overrun by zombie-like creatures known as "wanderers". Anyone even slightly familiar with Metal Gear as a franchise can point out how idiotic this concept is, yet the repetitive gameplay and egregious microtransactions took an already bad concept and made it into a true nightmare. Metal Gear hasn't had a fully original game since this release, and without Kojima at the helm, it's difficult to see any real future for the franchise.

1
'Ride to Hell: Retribution' (2013)

While every other game on this list was notoriously bad for the era, Ride to Hell: Retribution goes a step beyond in terms of terribly constructed gameplay and visuals to make for not just the worst game of the 2010s, but easily one of the worst video games of all time. The game sees the player as a hardened biker on a quest for revenge, taking down each member of the biker gang that killed his brother. Whether it be through awkward driving segments or terrible third-person shooter levels, Ride to Hell: Retribution is a glitchy, unplayable mess from beginning to end.

Even if the game were working as intended, its terrible visuals, laughably bad dialogue, and uninspired gameplay don't do anything to make the game worthwhile. The game even finds room to be outright misogynistic in its depiction of women as sex rewards for the player, just for good measure. It's one of the closest that a video game has gotten to recreating the feel of a so-bad-it's-good movie, where its failures are so abundant and in your face that one cannot help but laugh at the stupidity and low quality on display.

While not as immediately recognizable as other Mario games, the Paper Mario series has carved out a niche for itself thanks to the charm of its paper craft aesthetic and the simple fun of its gameplay. However, Paper Mario: Sticker Star completely forgoes the previous strengths of the series to create one of the largest dips in quality for any Nintendo franchise. While previous Paper Mario games created their own vast worlds with original characters and stories, Sticker Star abandons this for the basic Super Mario aesthetic that, while fun in a platforming setting, wasn't interesting to see in Paper Mario.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress%2Fwp-content%2Fauthors%2F672d316a30cbb-profile%20nov%202024.jpg?fit=crop&w=90&h=90

Even worse than these aesthetic choices is the game's primary combat mechanic, as instead of a simple yet layered RPG system or a fun 2D platformer in Super Paper Mario, Sticker Star's entire combat relies upon the collectible stickers. It's a JRPG without any XP, making every non-required fight an absolute waste of both time and resources. Its fights act more as puzzles instead of actual fights, yet when the puzzles are either incredibly easy or impossibly archaic to understand, the entire game becomes a test of patience and frustration.

8
'Umbrella Corps' (2016)

The continuous balancing act that has been done between the horror and action elements of the Resident Evil franchise has resulted in several misaligned failures that completely misunderstood the appeal and strengths of this franchise. However, none of these misfires are more infamous than Umbrella Corps, a tactical shooter that combines competitive multiplayer with zombies for an absolutely horrendous final product. The game had hopes of following in the footsteps of games like Rainbow Six Siege, yet no singular Resident Evil fan wanted a generic multiplayer shooter out of the franchise.

It's an incredibly forgettable first-person shooter game that has inklings of Resident Evil sprinkles placed over it, creating an experience that was never going to appeal to either Resident Evil fans or fans of traditional tactical shooters. With no interest in the game resulting in a hilariously low player count, the game failed as soon as it launched. Ironically, the game released a week after the announcement of Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, immediately painting the game as this awkward final reminder of when Resident Evil cared more about action than horror.

7
'Aliens: Colonial Marines' (2013)

Licensed tie-in video games are always a mixed bag of quality, yet Aliens: Colonial Marines in the lead-up to its release showed so much promise that gamers were expecting it to be one of the very best tie-in games. However, the game instead became one of the greatest examples of false advertising in video game history, with the final game having considerably worse graphics quality than trailers and even demos sent to the press.

Combined with an overwhelming amount of technical problems and bugs that made the game near-unplayable and an incredibly short length, Colonial Marines was the type of disastrous disappointment that sent ripples throughout the entire industry. It had some of the largest controversies and anger from fans of any video game of the 2010s, with there even being an attempted lawsuit being filed due to its false advertising. Hilariously enough, several of the game's flaws stemmed from developers Gearbox Software prioritizing the next game on this list instead of Colonial Marines.

6
'Duke Nukem Forever' (2011)

For over 14 years, Duke Nukem Forever has stood as this absolute icon of video game delays and the immediate go-to example of development hell and a game that was seemingly never going to be released. As it changed engines, developers, and platforms over the years, the game managed to finally get finished in 2011, when it not only disappointed fans but felt outright embarrassing to witness. It became immediately apparent that the crass humor and simplistic FPS gameplay that worked wonders in the 90s simply didn't land nearly as well in the 2010s.

blocks.c: A blonde woman holding the hand of a young little girl in a dark corridor in the video game 'Amy' for PS3 and Xbox 360

blocks.x: The game did surprisingly little to update the series and evolve it into the age of modern gaming, simply hoping that nostalgia and generic parody would be enough to entice long-time fans of this classic video game icon. Generic gameplay, tired clichés, and dated unfunny humor only served to annoy many modern gamers instead of charming them. It ended up being the final nail in the coffin for Duke as a character, as there hasn't been another Duke Nukem release in the 15 years since this game's monumental failure.

'Wreck-It Ralph' (2012)

Considering the fact that the fan-favorite Disney movie's entire concept and inception revolves around the fun and creativity of video games, it's all the more iconic and painful that the video game adaptation of Wreck-It Ralph is so abysmal in its execution. It's the clearest example of a cheap, made-for-profit movie tie-in game that the 2010s have to offer, with laughably bad cutscenes and the entire game able to be beaten in a few hours.

It certainly wants to pay tribute to some of the same 2D platformers that inspired the original movie, yet without any understanding of what made these games so great, the final product is a painfully generic mess of ideas that is forgotten by the time the credits roll. There is a sardonic humor to be had in the video game adaptation in a movie about video games being so poorly made, but even worse is the fact that this game wasn't even memorable in its lack of quality.

4
'Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 5' (2015)

The Tony Hawk's Pro Skater franchise was a pillar of quality in the early 2000s, at the apex of skateboarding video games and perfectly paralleling the renegade skater culture of the era. However, much like the declining popularity of skateboarding culture, the franchise largely fell out of popularity in the 2010s, with Activision releasing Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 5 at the literal last minute before their licensing deal with Tony Hawk would expire.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/ride_to_hell_retribution.png?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Two bikers riding motorcycles while aiming revolvers at each other in the video game 'Ride to Hell: Retribution'

blocks.x: As a result, Pro Skater 5 was hastily put together in a few months and released in a completely unfinished state, completely bastardizing a fan-favorite franchise and spitting in the face of fans who were waiting years for a new game in the series. It's an embarrassing case of profit-maximizing not only getting in the way of a game's success, but acting as the only reason for the game's very existence, creating a soulless husk of gaming and an incredibly disappointing sequel.

3
'Sonic Free Riders' (2010)

One seemingly inescapable trend of 2010s gaming that has largely gone by the wayside is the abundance of motion controls. Through the Nintendo Wii, PlayStation Move, and Xbox Kinect, every gaming studio was trying to create experiences tailored to non-gamers with physical motion as the main method of gameplay. While there were certainly games that found success, many failed to adapt to the concept, with one of the worst examples of such being Sonic Free Riders, a racing game requiring Kinect motion controls to play.

An unlikely candidate for what could be the worst game in the Sonic the Hedgehog franchise, Sonic Free Riders isn't just poorly made in its implementation of Kinect controls, but is outright unplayable with how unresponsive this control scheme is. Especially for a racing series that was previously defined by precision and slick tricks, the motion controls slow the feel of the game down to a crawl and make it an arduous task to even move.

While Metal Gear is massively celebrated as one of the greatest video game franchises out there, a great deal of its success and ingenuity is attributed to series creator Hideo Kojima. This meant that the separation of Kojima and Konami in 2015 placed the series in a state of unknown limbo, as it wouldn't be known what would happen to the series without Kojima's leadership. The answer ended up being Metal Gear Survive, which was worse than even the lowest expectations of what Metal Gear without Kojima would be.

Metal Gear Survive is a survival action game with tower-defense elements and minor stealth elements where the player explores a world overrun by zombie-like creatures known as "wanderers". Anyone even slightly familiar with Metal Gear as a franchise can point out how idiotic this concept is, yet the repetitive gameplay and egregious microtransactions took an already bad concept and made it into a true nightmare. Metal Gear hasn't had a fully original game since this release, and without Kojima at the helm, it's difficult to see any real future for the franchise.

1
'Ride to Hell: Retribution' (2013)

While every other game on this list was notoriously bad for the era, Ride to Hell: Retribution goes a step beyond in terms of terribly constructed gameplay and visuals to make for not just the worst game of the 2010s, but easily one of the worst video games of all time. The game sees the player as a hardened biker on a quest for revenge, taking down each member of the biker gang that killed his brother. Whether it be through awkward driving segments or terrible third-person shooter levels, Ride to Hell: Retribution is a glitchy, unplayable mess from beginning to end.

Even if the game were working as intended, its terrible visuals, laughably bad dialogue, and uninspired gameplay don't do anything to make the game worthwhile. The game even finds room to be outright misogynistic in its depiction of women as sex rewards for the player, just for good measure. It's one of the closest that a video game has gotten to recreating the feel of a so-bad-it's-good movie, where its failures are so abundant and in your face that one cannot help but laugh at the stupidity and low quality on display.

items.text:
The Lord of the Rings franchise is about to get an onslaught of new releases in the coming years, though not all of them are equally compelling, at least among longtime Tolkien fans. Middle-earth adaptations such as The Hunt for Gollum and The Rings of Power have been criticized for taking too many liberties with Tolkien's original material, even as both promise to take fans into beloved corners of the universe.

There is still plenty for fans to look forward to, however, with Middle-earth continuing to expand with projects like Colbert's Shadow of the Past, tabletop releases such as the new One Ring expansions, and more. Some will revisit familiar characters and periods of Tolkien history, while others are looking beyond the stories audiences have already seen adapted several times before. That varied slate could make the next few years one of the franchise's busiest periods yet, for better or worse, and the fanbase is by and large trying to remain cautiously optimistic.

However, one upcoming project is almost universally being hailed as the Middle-earth adaptation we've been waiting on for decades, and it will take the Lord of the Rings franchise in a completely new direction.

Lord Of The Rings Is Set To Make A Long Overdue Shift In Genre

The Lord of the Rings is about to make one of its boldest genre shifts yet, moving away from the film and television adaptations currently dominating the franchise and back toward a much more ambitious kind of interactive Middle-earth experience. As fans are well aware by now, Warhorse Studios, the developer behind Kingdom Come: Deliverance, officially confirmed in May 2026 that it is developing an open-world Middle-earth RPG, marking a new era for the IP.

That alone represents a dramatic change from the franchise's most recent major gaming release, Tales of the Shire, which approached Tolkien's world as a cozy life simulator. The game was an intentionally low-stakes interpretation of Middle-earth, prioritizing everyday life over the epic adventures normally associated with LOTR.

Warhorse appears to be heading in essentially the opposite direction. While virtually no gameplay details have been revealed yet, describing the project specifically as an open-world Middle-earth RPG immediately suggests a focus on discovery and free exploration, character progression, dangerous quests alongside an extensive main campaign, and player/character-driven adventures. Warhorse's pedigree makes that especially intriguing, considering Kingdom Come: Deliverance built its popularity around unusually detailed worlds and immersive role-playing systems.

After years of wildly different experiments with Tolkien's universe, Warhorse's project could finally give fans something they've been waiting on for decades: a dedicated, large-scale open-world RPG built around actually living out an adventure in Middle-earth.

The Wait For Warhorse's Middle-Earth RPG Will Be Worth It

Fans probably shouldn't expect Warhorse Studios' Lord of the Rings RPG anytime soon. The project remains extremely early in development and was only just announced, with no release date or window. An ambitious open-world interpretation of Middle-earth isn't exactly the kind of game that should be rushed, however. If Warhorse's history is any indication, though, giving the studio time will be well worth it in the long run.

Warhorse spent years establishing its approach to immersive RPG design with 2018's Kingdom Come: Deliverance, creating an open world built around historical authenticity, complicated gameplay systems, player choice, and an unusually grounded representation of medieval life. The studio then took nearly seven years to deliver Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2, and that patience paid off handsomely.

KCD 2 earned an 89 Metacritic score and currently holds a 92% positive rating across more than 67,000 English-language Steam reviews, showing just how far Warhorse's RPG formula has evolved and landed among the player-base.

Middle-earth could be an ideal setting and perfect match for Warhorse, as Tolkien's world would benefit from the small details, believable and intricate cultures, expansive landscapes, and the feeling that there's way more to discover beyond whatever quest the player happens to be focused on.

In other words, a lengthy development cycle isn't necessarily bad news, even if it means fans will have to sit tight for a while before immersing themselves in the experience. If Warhorse gives Middle-earth the same attention it gave medieval Bohemia, waiting several years could be a small price to pay for the kind of fully realized Lord of the Rings RPG fans have wanted for decades.

items.text:
I've had this goal in the back of my head to unlock all the Medic gear in Wardogs so I can become the best sawbones on the server. There's only one piece I still don't have—a medical bag that can both revive and heal teammates in one item. It's unlocked at Medic level 24, which doesn't sound so bad, since I've already reached level 18 over my first 30 hours of Wardogs.

But this week I noticed my steady Medic rise had slowed considerably. I had been ranking up every one or two rounds, but now I'm lucky to climb a rank over a whole night of play. I'm doing just as well in matches—better than ever, actually, with the addition of defibrillators and stronger medkits—so that's not the issue.

For the first time, I made note of the XP thresholds for leveling up and compared where I'm at to my goal. I wish I hadn't. So far I've gained 17 levels with 177,619 Medic XP. Level 24, just seven ranks later, will require 337,000 XP. So while it looks like I'm gaining on that useful medicine bag, I'm actually just 52% of the way there.

So this is the brutal Wardogs grind I've been hearing about. Bummer.

The mountain

I was curious how that last 48% will translate to playtime and matches—maybe it'll go by faster than it sounds—so I did an unscientific test: I played an average match with my typical focus on revives and healing. For the record: I'm an OK player at best. To maximise XP gains, I also brought an SMG and purchased stims to administer to teammates.

Over a 50-minute match on the winning team, this was my scoreline:

Medic XP earned

Cash earned

Revives

Kills

Assists

9,995

$62,215

15 (2nd highest)

2

5

A pretty low kill game, admittedly. Our team repeatedly pulled the zone to our walled-off FOB, so there was a lot of time spent dragging bodies away from mortar barrages. If I keep playing like this, I'd unlock the medicine bag in 16 more matches, or ~13 hours of playtime.

I reckon that, depending on who you are, that either sounds surprisingly reasonable or totally deflating. It's disheartening for me, because these days I only play games for two or three hours on the nights that I play anything at all. By my standards, I've been going hard on Wardogs these past two weeks and yet I'm still at least a week away from unlocking this singular item.

Is this mountainous XP climb exactly what Bulkhead had in mind, and if so, is it good? It's a question the Wardogs community is grappling with every day, and opinions are all over the map. Some think the XP milestones increase too quickly, others think the grind would be fine if not for the planned seasonal wipes, and some firmly believe that Wardogs needs its massive XP grind to stay interesting.

(Image credit: Team17)It's an issue of degrees. To what degree is Wardogs meant to accommodate players with limited time, and how much should Bulkhead cater to the diehards racking up hundreds of hours? Complex multiplayer games have a way of splintering into differing perceived states depending on the beholder's skill and commitment level.

Changing the state of XP and cash is both a philosophical and balancing consideration: If it takes less XP to get my precious medicine bag or RPG or attack helicopter, that also affects how quickly powerful items become prominent in matches throughout a season, and Wardogs' meta progression flattens. But if nothing changes, then a player at my level may never unlock some items before the next wipe—fair, but not fun in the long term.

Bulkhead is taking in all the feedback around grind, and has alluded to future features that will shake up the grind from season-to-season, but hasn't commented on specific changes yet. Its first major patch since early access launch is still a few weeks away—season 2 begins October 15, and will wipe everyone back to level 1. Back to the base of the mountain.

items.title: There Are Only Two Things That Money Can’t Buy: True Love, And Homegrown Tomatoes
items.author: Rebekah Valentine
items.summary: Everyone who knows me even somewhat closely has, in the last few years, had to listen to me gush about how much I love participating in a farm share program.
items.text:
Everyone who knows me even somewhat closely has, in the last few years, had to listen to me gush about how much I love participating in a farm share program. In winter, I pay a sizeable (but reasonable for what I get) quantity of money to a local farm to help fund their seeds and such. Then, starting in spring, every week I drive 20 minutes to that farm and am handed a big box of whatever the heck they happen to be harvesting at the time.

Fresh, local produce rules. It’s encouraged me to expand my cooking repertoire and try new foods, and I generally think everything I get tastes noticeably better than out-of-season nonsense from the big grocery store. I’ve had some of the best apples of my life this way, learned and loved the humble pawpaw fruit, and developed a begrudging respect for most greens (I still can’t get onboard with kale).

Also, tomatoes. Tomatoes! Did you know homegrown (or, well, grown at a small farm 20 minutes from home) tomatoes are…delicious?

Now, I’ve disliked tomatoes for most of my life. Watery and bland on their own, or sometimes sour or mushy and unpleasant. I avoided them if at all possible. I’ve made my views on ketchup clear elsewhere. Pasta sauce is tolerable if made well, but fresh tomatoes? Get those right out of here.

Well, what I’ve discovered from this farm share is that when you eat tomatoes fresh and in-season within spitting distance of where they’ve been grown, they’re incredible. Sure, it’s only for a few months each year, but wow! Juicy, tangy, even a little umami going on? I slice ’em and fry ’em on a cast iron and sprinkle ’em with a little Maldon seasoning salt. I toss ’em on a grilled cheese sandwich for a bit of an acidic punch. When I get lots, I cook them down into incredible pasta sauce or oven roast them with a little olive oil and mash them into salsa with some of the peppers that usually show up in the share alongside them. There are big, fat tomatoes for slicing and putting on burgers, and little grape-sized ones I can just pop in my mouth with no prep needed.

Oh, God, and if you manage to get one fresh? Right off the vine? Sun-warmed? Holy tomato, guys, what a dream!

Homegrown tomatoes! Homegrown tomatoes!

Why are we talking about tomatoes today? Well, this morning, I heard this song on the radio:

Well, you can go out to eat and that’s for sure
But it’s nothin’ a homegrown tomato won’t cure
Put ’em in a salad, put ’em in a stew
You can make your very own tomato juice
You can eat ’em with eggs, you can eat ’em with gravy
Eat ’em with beans, pinto or navy
Put ’em on the side, put ’em in the middle
Put a homegrown tomato on a hotcake griddle

This guy gets it! I can’t believe I’ve never heard this song before! “Homegrown Tomatoes” is by country singer Guy Clark, apparently one of his better-known songs, which makes it all the more embarrassing for me that I hadn’t known about it. I spend most of my time listening to sad-girl indie songs about yearning and when-will-my-husband-return-from-the-war, so the idea that you can spend a whole song rightfully extolling the virtues of the homegrown tomato has me just elated. Did you all know that you can just do that? Are there more excellent, wholesome songs about the general deliciousness of food items out there that I can listen to?

We’re unfortunately approaching the very tail end of tomato season, and I’m seeing fewer and fewer of them in my farm share each week. There were none in the most recent pick-up. It might be over. The tomato in the photo up top is the last one I have from two shares ago. I’m not even out and I miss them already.

What shall I do with this last homegrown tomato? There is, according to the very wise Guy Clark, no wrong answer:

Homegrown tomatoes, homegrown tomatoes
What’d life be without homegrown tomatoes?
Only two things that money can’t buy
And that’s true love and homegrown tomatoes

Have a lovely weekend, everyone! I hope you get to try a homegrown tomato yourself before it gets too cold for them. It’ll be a long, long winter without homegrown tomatoes, but they’ll come back again next year. They always do.

items.author: Natalia Keogan
items.summary: Taking even a cursory pulse-check of the pitfalls of modern technology—burgeoning AI sentience, data-center-induced draughts, massive quantities of unprocessed
items.text:
Taking even a cursory pulse-check of the pitfalls of modern technology—burgeoning AI sentience, data-center-induced draughts, massive quantities of unprocessed e-waste—will provoke an uneasy question: Did the Unabomber kind of have a point? This, of course, refers to the FBI code name (standing for University and Airline Bomber) for Ted Kaczynski. The man penned a 35,000-word manifesto entitled Industrial Society And Its Future, which, if it weren’t accompanied by a deadly mail bomb campaign, would likely endure as an articulate warning of the corporate-backed, man-made horrors of our current industrial hellscape.


Instead, Kaczynski’s legacy is inextricable from the three deaths and multiple injuries he caused as part of a calculated effort, between 1978 and 1995, to eliminate those he deemed responsible for what he saw as the fast-approaching erosion of natural and human rights in favor of technological evolution. The 1994 murder of advertising executive Thomas J. Mosser in North Caldwell, New Jersey (yes, where The Sopranos house is located) opens Janus Metz Pedersen’s Netflix biopic Unabomber, but the film is much more invested in the making of this murderer than the mechanics of his crimes.


Unabomber toggles back and forth between FBI agent Joanne Miller’s (Shailene Woodley) efforts to capture Kaczynski in 1996—ending what was at the time the longest and most expensive investigation ever spearheaded by the bureau—and Kaczynski’s formative time at Harvard as a precocious math prodigy (Jacob Tremblay) in the late ’50s. Between these two timelines, there is a palpable tension between prioritizing entertainment or accuracy. For one, Miller is a complete fabrication, a beguiling choice considering that the film delves into the very real role that Kaczynski’s brother played in his eventual arrest by the FBI. This version of the Unabomber—an unkempt, paranoid recluse residing in the Montana wilderness—is hardly ever seen. Instead, we get to know the man as a gangly, insecure student, completely adrift within academia and his general place in the world.


While not necessarily common knowledge, there has been quite a bit of research into the impact that studying at Harvard had on Kaczynski, particularly as it pertains to an ethically dubious psychological study conducted by professor Henry Murray (a flat Russell Crowe) that he participated in. It would appear that Unabomber largely leans on Harvard And The Making Of The Unabomber by Alston Chase (who attended the school at the same time as Kaczynski), which exposes the cruelty that the young man was subjected to while enrolled in the study. In the wake of the Korean War, Professor Murray sought to prove whether a man’s firmest beliefs can be upheld even under intense emotional stress. (“I bet you just look down at that tiny little dick of yours and just wish it would fall off,” sneers an unpleasant anonymous interviewer at Kaczynski during one such experiment.) As it turns out, efforts to assess an impervious American attitude ended up backfiring, big time. The key thesis of Chase’s book—the research of which includes intensive correspondence with an incarcerated Kaczynski—is that his 200 hours spent as a test subject effectively turned him against science and society writ large, pushing him to resort to violence as a means of direct action.


Yet the most compelling components of this text aren’t really present in Unabomber, which nods toward identifying details of the experiment but shirks from engaging with its psychological implications. Rather, banal story beats rely too heavily on Kaczynski’s dating difficulties and inherent introversion, and not how these already present insecurities may have been intensified. Indeed, even long after his capture, Kaczynski struggled with his mental health, eventually dying by suicide in 2023 at the age of 81. Instead of delving into the full breadth of Kaczynski’s psychological background, Unabomber is content with generic “abusive dad” flashbacks and simplified “frigid mother” anecdotes.


A Netflix dramatization of Kaczynski’s life, no matter the time period, would never be as faithful or scrutinizing as would be necessary to engage with the legacy of the Unabomber. Frankly, a project that actually engaged with his philosophy would probably result in a good deal of subscribers being put on government watchlists. But it’s nonetheless quasi-insulting that the film ends with a recorded interview with Kaczynski, in which he states, in a disarmingly soft voice: “My personal preference is to be depicted truthfully…To me, the main thing is to get rid of the industrial system by whatever means necessary.” For a film that is neither particularly truthful nor sympathetic to Kaczynski’s desperate need to question the cost of technological advancement, it’s an odd—if accidentally resonant—note to end on.


Director: Janus Metz Pedersen

Writer: Sam Chalsen, Nelson Greaves

Starring: Russell Crowe, Jacob Tremblay, Annabelle Wallis, Shailene Woodley

Release Date: September 25, 2026 (Netflix)

items.author: Zack Zwiezen

items.text:
I love Star Wars and play a lot of Star Wars games. Some are good. Some are bad. But so many of them are either shooters or third-person action games. Those can be fun, sure, but the Star Wars universe can support so much more than that. So I’m very excited about Star Wars: Galactic Racer, an upcoming fast-paced arcade racer with some roguelike elements. And its arrival just a few weeks after Zero Company hopefully marks the start of more Star Wars games doing something different.

Galactic Racer, out on October 6 on PS5, Xbox, and PC, is the first game from Fuse Games, a studio founded by some key folks behind the fantastically fast Burnout franchise. And I mean, the idea of some former Burnout devs and leaders working on a new racing game is an exciting prospect in and of itself. But the fact that Galactic Racer is also set in the Star Wars universe and will feature podracing and iconic planets like Tatooine makes it sound like this game could be very special.

When you think about it, Star Wars and racing seem like a perfect match. Heck, back in the day we got a few Star Wars–themed racing games (and even a Twisted Metal knock-off). So what happened? Why did they stop getting made?

Why did it take this long for a new Star Wars racing game?

It doesn’t all have to be Lego game, shooter, third-person thingy. items.text:
“It’s embarrassing to know so little about something that occupies so much of your visual environment.” A little over ten minutes into his film, “The History of Concrete,” director John Wilson shares these words in praise of that very material that so many of us trample on without thinking twice. His project offers that second look, a reminder that there’s no better way to move through the world than to be guided by curiosity, bolstered by the hope that stories can be found in the most unlikely places.

Wilson operates from a place of disarming honesty and, at the start of his film, admits that the success he got from the comedy docu-series “How To with John Wilson,” like the blemishes of gum on the NYC pavement, isn’t without its blemishes. In the midst of a difficult search to find a worthy follow-up project, he attends a workshop on how to write a Hallmark movie.

After watching one film called “’Twas the Date Before Christmas,” which tried to “fit a romance inside of a topic as unromantic as affordable housing,” he decides to pair the tried and true tactics of Hallmark movies with a subject that might test the limits of their effectiveness: making a project about concrete.

As is par for the course for Wilson’s projects, his work starts as one thing and quickly finds itself off the beaten path, touching on everything from the unique grieving rituals (key words: “tattooed flesh embalming”), the terrifying infrastructures (the BQE bridge) that we have made peace living with, and ultimately, about the things in life that will last and what’s worth patching up.

For Wilson, the film continues his commitment to finding interesting stories rooted in things most people would often overlook (or, in the case of concrete, just step over). “I’m a maximalist in a lot of ways, and I think being curious makes you less bored,” he shared.

As “The History of Concrete” expands, RogerEbert.com spoke with him about humanity’s penchant for creating new grieving rituals, the virtue of curiosity, and the discernment process behind a project like this, with so many footage options to choose from.

This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

You port over your same “don’t show the host, only play the voice,” tactic from “How To with John Wilson.” Tell me more about your approach to narration, since when you’re recording your words, they’re divorced from where you were when you filmed the footage.

John Wilson: It can be quite fickle and dependent on mood. It’s very much a Jacob’s ladder type of process. In the case of something like my show, I usually start with a title, then try to shoot a few things relevant to the title itself.

So with something like “The History of Concrete,” I wanted to “get all the vegetables” out of the way, so to speak, which is why I included a couple of students who knew the difference between cement and concrete and could explain it. As I’m shooting, certain things will either happen to me in real life or will enter me emotionally, and I will need to write that into the script. I will look at all the footage and write a script on top of it so I’m constantly editing, writing, and shooting at the same time.

I’m wondering about how you choose to match footage with your words because the ways in which what we see on-screen contradicts what’s spoken–and when they align–are fascinating to take note of. The scene where you talk about the poor foundations of buildings like your gym is “making people really upset because the city doesn’t seem to acknowledge the problem.” You intersperse that with a humorous video of someone mollywopping an exercise ball.

That’s an example where it helps to have something as uniquely specific as that visual to build around. I started with this desire to use the shot of the gym flooding, then I was thinking, “Okay, what else do I have from this environment?” That is kind of the template I use for the sequences you see in the film going forward: I have a kernel of an idea, and then I try to either find something I already have or shoot something new that adds a punchline. I try to use the rule of threes when I can when writing certain sequences, but you don’t always need a punchline at the same time.

On that note of discernment, you talked about how, when making a feature, there are no time constraints apart from “consideration for the audience.” With your show, you were constrained by the straitjacket of twenty-eight minutes, but what guides you and editor Cori Wapnowska’s process when you have a cornucopia of footage to work with?

That first cut is really messy and has everything in it, and when I’m looking at what I’ve assembled, I am able to see the whole picture, where the actual emotional turns are and what the plot is. That version of the film also helps me determine which strong sequences, in isolation, I can build the film around and what can support the crescendo to those moments.

I try not to have any redundant revelations or ideas in the film. The temptation can be to double up, but I try to hold fast to that. If I repeat any beats, I want to reveal slightly different information in whatever comes next. For the most part, even if an interview feels like a non-sequitur, it needs to rhyme with something else in the film, or its inclusion needs to strengthen the film thematically by reinforcing a particular metaphor.

For example, there’s that sequence where I document a military exercise that takes place out of a high school at one point. You can take that as just an observation that I happened to tag on, but some of the intentionality there was to show how that fits in with this recurring theme of rule-following, our obsession with structure and order, and what it is about ourselves as a species that we feel a need to be told what to do.

Beyond those questions, one thing that felt like it unified “The History of Concrete” was your documentation of how people cannot help but use rituals to process grief and loss. It’s such a small part of the film, but I’m struck by that community that held a vigil for the fish that were killed when their pond was filled with concrete.

Yeah, I mean, we showcase Chef Boyardee’s grave here. I think death and fatality is a kind of recurring background theme in a lot of the work that I end up making. I think that there can be the death of a physical person, but I think there’s the death of civic space and these larger industries around us all the time, and we have different ceremonies for that. It feels like the new public ceremony is almost “protest for mourning.”

I feel like there are cultures that just kind of put you in a pine box, and it’s very unflashy, but then you have this industry of tattoo preservation where it feels like you’re mummifying somebody. I like, I’m constantly debating in my own life whether or not I should be sad about something disappearing or if I should be trying to figure out ways emotionally to deal with the disappearance of something. Looking at the different ways that other cultures grieve is a big part of that education.

Doesn’t it feel overwhelming, though, to know how to properly lament when it feels like the scale of things we should mourn for outstrips our ability to comprehend what we might be losing?

Yes, but this movie is dealing with a thousand-year timeline. I’m trying to acknowledge humans as grains of sand in this endless, infinite time. I try not to zoom out too far just because I need to keep the point sharpened to a degree.

It makes me think, though: what does a thousand-year city look like? How are we to live our lives on Earth knowing that we only have so much time here? It seems like many people’s answer is to engage in cyclical behavior. Is that something market forces determine and force on us, or something we naturally do to get through existing? I wonder if there’s a better way.

It ties back to that line your subject mentions about the BQE’s crumbling infrastructure: “We’re aware of a flaw but are incapable of stopping it.”

But are we really incapable of stopping it? I ultimately try to contain myself within a timeline that I can mentally comprehend, but that yields its own interesting challenges. It’s funny, because I was talking to the people who were in the tattoo preservation business, and I asked a couple of people in different interviews that weren’t in the movie, essentially, “What do you plan to do with this [business] after you pass away?” There’s no plan for that.

It becomes this act of kicking the can of preservation and legacy just further down the road. think people tend to think within a hundred years of their life, usually, or maybe even less. I think that’s mostly what you can comprehend because when you start to think about 10,000 years from now, it’s just like, “Why am I doing anything?”

When I look at your projects and the way you deploy humor, you often use it as a kind of weapon to subvert the dynamics of who holds power. By highlighting the absurdity of our existence, your humor calls into question the aforementioned market forces that shape our lives. How do you feel this idea has expanded with a project like “The History of Concrete?”

I think about that all the time. I try to be right on the razor’s edge as often as I can of what’s okay and what’s not, because I think that’s where a lot of the best comedy and art lies. I think humor can be an instrument to speak truth to power, and if I’m punching, I always try to punch up. I think there are some obvious villains out in the world that everyone can usually laugh at, whether it’s a cop doing something funny or even just the mayor, no matter how popular the mayor is. I think it’s pretty timeless to have an antagonistic relationship with the mayor in certain ways for a lot of New Yorkers.

Landlords too, which, as you’re a landlord, speaks to your willingness to fall on the blade yourself.

Yeah; I occupy a complicated place within the city that I acknowledge, and I try to lacerate myself in equal measure to a lot of the people within capital “P” politics.

I’m speaking to you in the middle of TIFF, and there’s a film that premiered, “Babies,” where a character played by Seth Rogen critiques the ways we praise babies for being “curious” when the only reason they’re curious is that they don’t know anything.

(Laughs) Yeah, I can relate.

That connects in some ways to what I feel is the thematic spine of this project because you say this line. “Once you’re used to something, it becomes kind of hard to change your lifestyle without external pressure.” It’s so easy to move through the world, simply accepting things as they are, and we lose that childlike curiosity. What helps you stay curious?

I tend to try to just run in a direction that nobody else is running in. I feel like I can’t work fast enough a lot of the time. There are just so many interesting and funny things to comment on and to explore within human relationships, and humanity’s relationship with the environment. You can literally pick anything … you can throw a dart at a board of words and just pick one, and then that’s your new obsession. You can find a galaxy within any one of those things.

There are a lot of things I want to see fixed in the city. I think a lot of New Yorkers have a signature thing they gripe about, and it ends up consuming their lives. Making art about something you would like to see improved will never get old.

In so many ways, I think part of me feels like I accidentally made this movie, and other parts of me feel like it was always meant to happen. I think it’s surreal that we’re talking about it right now and that what I’ve crafted is in any condition to analyze. I’m a maximalist in a lot of ways, and I think being curious makes you less bored. It makes you actually understand your environment rather than just passively walking through it.

Waking up from the matrix can be frustrating, but it’s also cool because it connects you with other people. I don’t know; meeting the world with your curiosity renews your faith in humanity in a certain way and helps you engage in things that you weren’t engaged in before.
